skyline.text: How a tariff moves money from the poor to the rich
Ajay Shah on Deng Xiaoping, and his pick for greatest human
Hayek’s essay on how prices run an economy without planners

brief.head: Opiate of the asses
brief.text: Conspiracy theories, Ajay Shah said, are “the opiate of the asses”: the world is so complicated that to believe one, you have to be simple-minded. {006-J03}

brief.head: Slogans beat stories
brief.text: Populists win on simplistic narratives, Amit Varma argued. Trump’s 2016 story of lost jobs, “China bad”, was appealing but false; the complex truth makes no slogan. {006-C04}

brief.head: Safety before plenty
brief.text: Safety and freedom come before prosperity, Ajay Shah argued, so Deng Xiaoping’s record is open to question. Amit Varma replied that escaping poverty is an absolute value. {006-C10}

brief.head: Two candlesticks
brief.text: Amit Varma was the first person to win the Bastiat Prize twice. Its trophy, a candlestick, nods to the candlemakers who petitioned to block out the sun. {006-S02}

brief.head: A 19th-century man
brief.text: Ajay Shah counts himself part of economics’ 19th-century tradition, closer to the dreams of Ricardo, Adam Smith and Marx. Today’s economics, he said, is “a pale shadow”. {006-J19}

thought.who: Amit Varma, who likes to alliterate, on why capitalism is the opposite of cronyism

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on Bastiat and Hayek
lead.head: Two Freddies and a broken window
body: Amit Varma named his friend Freddie after two heroes: the 19th-century French writer Frédéric Bastiat and the economist Friedrich Hayek. In this episode he and Ajay Shah told Freddie’s deep, dark backstory.

Between them, the two Freddies offer a way of seeing the world. Bastiat taught that every policy has effects you can see and effects you cannot. Hayek showed why no planner can know enough to run an economy, and why prices do the job instead.

Bastiat’s parable of the broken window sets the pattern. People say a broken window is good for the economy, because the glazier gets paid. {#window} What is not seen, Varma said, is what the owner would have done with that money: bought a coat, perhaps, or a cake.
A bad economist, he said, looks only at first-order effects. A good one takes everything into account.
## From the poor to the rich

From that habit of mind, Varma drew his central claim. “Most government interventions in the economy, in the market, if not all, redistribute wealth from the poor to the rich,” he said. He wanted it in capital letters. {006-C05}

Tariffs are a great example, he said. Shield a local teddy-bear maker from a cheaper Chinese rival, and each buyer pays ten rupees more. Each barely notices the loss; the local lobby collects the lot.

Shah added a darker twist. Blowing up a railroad or a port would raise costs once and for all. A tariff can be granted or withdrawn, industry by industry, giving the state “Godlike power over the entrepreneurial class”. {006-C06}
Bastiat called it plunder when people seize what others produce. When honest profit is too hard, Varma said, people seek rent instead.
## Makers and takers

Shah took the argument to China. There, he said, party-connected takers have repeatedly used state power against makers, until entrepreneurs learned to put party members on their boards and princelings among their shareholders.
“A government that will give you anything that you want is a government that can take away everything that you have,” he said.
Shah also offered a hopeful counterpoint. Jeff Bezos’s *Washington Post* went after Donald Trump, and the President could neither shut it down nor hit back at Bezos. {006-S08}
## Prices as messengers

Hayek’s essay *The Use of Knowledge in Society* answered calls for a central committee to set every price. The knowledge an economy runs on, Shah explained, is scattered across everyone: one person’s need for a taxi, another’s willingness to drive. No planner can gather it all.

Prices coordinate everyone without anyone needing to talk. Varma keeps returning to Uber’s surge pricing, which lets those who value a ride most pay for it and calls an idle driver out from his lunch.
Cap the price and the scarcity stays; only the supply vanishes. “People simply don’t realise that you cannot legislate scarcity away,” Varma said. {006-C14}
The hosts ended with books. Shah chose Milton Friedman’s *Capitalism and Freedom*, whose chapters each struck him “like an earthquake”; Varma, Henry Hazlitt’s *Economics in One Lesson*.

Capitalism, Varma said, equals consent: many people acting voluntarily in double thank-you moments, where buyer and seller both come out ahead. It is often confused with cronyism, he added, which is its opposite.

second.label: Frédéric Bastiat
second.head: All the breath he had
second.deck: Amit Varma on the French economist who died at 49, his own age
body: Frédéric Bastiat, the 19th-century French writer, economist and parliamentarian, died at 49. That, Amit Varma noted sadly, is his own age. {#fortynine}

Bastiat caught tuberculosis while travelling around France to popularise his ideas. Knowing his lungs were failing, and referring, Varma thinks, to his book *The Law*, he vowed to proclaim his principle until the day of his death. {006-S01}

The economist Joseph Schumpeter called him the most brilliant economic journalist who ever lived. {006-J13} Varma said Bastiat explained ideas like opportunity cost before such terms were in much use, and wondered what he could have done with many more years. Ajay Shah’s consolation: Varma has fifty more years, and owes the world “five big books”.

quote.text: I shall proclaim this principle with all the force of my lungs, which alas is all too inadequate.

second.caption: Bastiat’s last campaign

third.head: Jeeps, judges and Indira
body: Raj Narain, Ajay Shah recalled, dragged Indira Gandhi to Justice Sinha’s courtroom in the Allahabad High Court over a “sweet little problem”: using some government jeeps for campaigning. {006-S06}

The point, Shah said, was the separation. There is the Congress party and there is the government, and the government owns the jeeps. Use them to campaign and your election is invalidated. That, he said, was India in 1975.
“We in India should be very, very proud,” he said. “Don’t you love it?”

China has never had such constitutional niceties, Shah argued. There the party is the state and the state is the party. {#partystate} Its businesses learned, in time, to serve at the pleasure of the party.
third.caption: Indira Gandhi and the government jeeps

p2.title: Unseen and unplanned
p2.deck: Frédéric Bastiat on the unseen, Friedrich Hayek on the price system, as argued over by Amit Varma and Ajay Shah

sections.label: Bastiat’s lens
sections.head: The coat nobody bought
sections.caption: the seen and the unseen
body: Frédéric Bastiat’s essay *That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen* opens with a broken window. Onlookers say it is good for the economy, because the man who repairs it gets paid. {#window}
That is what is seen, Amit Varma said. What is not seen is what the owner would have done with the money had it been left with him: bought a coat, say, or a cake.

The same fallacy, he said, lies behind the argument that war is good for the economy. {#war} Such consequences are often unintended, but not unforeseen: once you understand economic laws, you can foresee many of them.
## Ditches and surprises

Varma applies the lens to GDP. He objects to counting government spending in it, an argument he said Keynes and others won before the Second World War. A government could tax people to dig ditches and fill them, and GDP would keep growing. “And every metric can be gamed,” he said. {006-C02}
Ajay Shah traced the idea to the sociologist Robert K. Merton, in 1936, he seemed to think: all purposive social action has unintended consequences. {#merton}
Beyond the obvious effects, Shah said, the world will surprise us: “we only dimly understand the full consequences of all-purposive social action.” {006-C03}
~ Varma’s first plan for his own podcast, *The Seen and the Unseen*, was short episodes on public policies, busting one fallacy at a time.

quote.text: A bad economist will only look at your first order effect. But a good economist will take everything into account

sections.label: Poor to rich
sections.head: Robin Hood runs backwards
sections.caption: tariffs and the teddy bear
body: Frédéric Bastiat’s genius, Amit Varma said, was to distil complex ideas into stories everybody could understand. In *The Candlemakers’ Petition*, the candlemakers ask whoever ruled France to block out the sun. {#candles}
Another satire seeks a ban on working with the right hand, since more effort was supposed to mean more prosperity. A third answers foreign competition by destroying the railroads. {#railroads}
Varma’s modern version involves teddy bears. A local maker sells at 100 rupees; a Chinese rival sells at 90. The government puts a 20-rupee tariff on the import, which now costs 110. {#tariff}
Ten rupees moves from each buyer to the local maker, who also loses the incentive to raise his game. Public choice theory calls this diffuse costs and concentrated benefits. {#diffuse}
## A sword over business
Ajay Shah asked why a state would choose tariffs over blowing up a railroad or the JNPT, India’s biggest container port, when the effect on prices is the same. {#jnpt}

Blowing up the port is a one-time decision, he said. A tariff can be granted, removed or brought back, industry by industry, leaving capitalists dangling. That beats a simple transfer from the poor to the rich.
~ Follow the incentives, Varma added, and party positions make sense. The AAP opposes FDI in retail, and many of its biggest supporters are small retailers.

quote.text: So the cost is diffused among a large variety of people. I lose 10 rupees, I won’t even notice.

sections.label: Two ways to get rich
sections.head: Plunder by permit
sections.caption: makers, takers and refuge
body: In *The Law*, Frédéric Bastiat named two ways to live: by applying your own faculties, the origin of property, or by seizing what others produce, the origin of plunder. Today, Amit Varma said, plunder mostly runs through the coercive power of the state, as rent-seeking and cronyism.

Jagdish Bhagwati once said, Varma recalled, that the Chinese were turning out to be profit-seeking and Indians rent-seeking. Varma does not know enough about China to judge, but for India it rings true.

People choose whichever path is less burdensome, Bastiat argued. “If it is easier to seek profit, you will seek profit,” Varma said. {006-C07} In India’s first decades honest trade was too hard, and a rent-seeking mentality took hold.
## The price of refuge

Ajay Shah’s terms were makers and takers. Makers build products and organisations that serve consumers. Takers grab, and once the state holds a monopoly on violence, they grab through regulations and rules.
Protection from the state, Shah said, always costs something, in unpredictable demands that come later. {006-C08}

~ Bastiat’s dystopia, Varma replied, is the modern world, where the state is all-powerful and the makers fight against the odds. Bastiat would have recognised India and China, he said, and Russia with some horror.

quote.text: Every form of refuge has a price.

sections.label: Hayek’s prices
sections.head: The fare that finds a driver
sections.caption: surge pricing and price caps
body: Friedrich Hayek’s *The Use of Knowledge in Society*, which Amit Varma called the most important and seminal essay of the twentieth century, argued against Oscar Lange’s proposal for a central price committee. {006-J15}
Frédéric Bastiat had made a similar point about Paris, Varma said. No committee decides who eats what, yet the city, almost miraculously and without coordination, feeds itself.

Varma’s everyday example is Uber. If 200 people want cabs and only 20 are available, a price cap hands them to the first 20, even someone casually off to the mall while another needs a hospital. {#taxis}
Surge pricing lets those who value a ride most pay for it. More important, Varma said, it signals an idle driver to come out and make money by serving others. {006-C13}
## No law against scarcity
Price controls always lead to shortages, he said. Decree that a car should cost no more than ten thousand, and existing cars are snapped up and production stops. {#cars}

About three years before the recording, Delhi’s AAP government had just experimented with a price cap on Uber when a friend of Varma’s could not get a cab to the airport and missed his flight. {006-S04}
~ When the government capped the price of stents, Varma predicted shortages and deaths. “Exactly that happened,” he said.

quote.text: The price carried information, the price carried an incentive, and more and more cabs get on the street because they want to make money

sections.label: Order without design
sections.head: No one ordered this pencil
sections.caption: discovery, not design
body: Many beautiful things, Amit Varma said, are what Adam Ferguson called “the product of human action but not human design”: the way cities and economies function, the way languages evolve, even natural selection. {006-J16}
Ajay Shah prefers a phrase from mathematics and science, the self-organising system: local decisions, no central control, remarkable results.

Friedrich Hayek’s insight, Shah said, has two parts. The knowledge of preferences and circumstances is dispersed across society, so “a planner will always get it wrong”. And prices coordinate us, so nobody need agree who plays Hamlet and who plays Ophelia. {006-C12}
## The conceit returns

If the twentieth century taught one bumper-sticker lesson, Shah said, it is that central planning brings stagnation. Yet the computer revolution keeps reviving the planner’s dream, a game of whack-a-mole. “We should let the world be a process of discovery, not design,” he said. {006-C11}

Varma recalled Adam Smith’s “man of system”, who imagines he can treat the world like a board of chess. Leonard Read’s essay *I, Pencil* shows the opposite: a pencil’s parts come from some forty or fifty countries, from people who never talk to one another. {#pencil}
~ For Shah, a card-carrying economist, the price system is the heart and soul of economics. He would have COVID vaccines traded on free markets, with futures contracts.

quote.text: We are all AGIs that are walking this planet trying to do things for ourselves.

side.boxText: Amit Varma’s podcast, *The Seen and the Unseen*, is inspired by Bastiat’s essay *That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen*. It begins with the parable of the broken window and asks you to look past a policy’s visible effect. {006-R01}

contQuote.text: I keep telling people that what is capitalism? It’s the voluntary actions of many people coming together. You’re playing positive sum games. It’s double thank you moments.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: From a Chinese boardroom to a Gujarat village, and what each one teaches

stories.start: the clearest place where we can see this playing out is China
stories.end: unlimited prerogative of imposing infinite taxation upon the so-called rich people
stories.caption: China’s makers and takers
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on China’s makers, takers and princelings
stories.head: The princeling on the board
body: In Ajay Shah’s telling, China’s entrepreneurs met their state in stages. At first there was some genuine promise. {#phaseone} You could have an idea, find cool technology, serve the consumer, build a complex organisation and make money, fair and square.
But in China there is not much of a line between the state and the Chinese Communist Party. “The party is the state and the state is the party,” Shah said.

Then, again and again, takers used state power against makers. A maker would be driven into distress and sell a perfectly nice business for a song, or be forced to shut down while the taker grabbed the market.

Capitalists got the point. In what Shah thinks of as the last 15 years, any significant business has needed party members on its board, or princelings, the children of party leaders, as shareholders. {#fifteen}

He voiced the pragmatic entrepreneur. “Chodo yaar, I have to get three party people as my board members. I’ll do it.” Twenty per cent of the shares to a princeling? No problem: he keeps his 80 per cent, and the fixing has been done. {#princeling}

Such protection is never free, Shah said: a state that can give you anything can take everything away. {006-S07} Demands follow at unpredictable dates, from “give this guy a job” to changing how a product is run. It amounts to taxation not codified in law, as before the Magna Carta, and China has had an investment slump.
~ Russia, he said, is a step further. There Putin decides whether an oligarch goes to jail, is sent into exile or is murdered in London.
stories.why: Wealth means little unless it can stand up to the state. Entrepreneurs who accept the fixing, Shah argued, are not thinking two moves ahead; to be in business, he said, you need to be a philosopher.
stories.postscript: Shah’s hopeful counterexample: Jeff Bezos’s *Washington Post* went after Donald Trump, and the federal government could not hit back. {006-S08}

stories.start: I remember in circa 93 or uh whenever the the there was an earthquake
stories.end: buy uh bread so everybody gets a couple of slices to eat
stories.caption: bread after the earthquake
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on bread prices after a Gujarat earthquake
stories.head: Dear bread, shared bread
body: Around 1993 or 1994, Amit Varma, then a student, volunteered after an earthquake in Gujarat and rode in an ambulance with a bunch of paramedics. {006-S03}
They stopped at a village where all the buildings had collapsed. A couple of shops were open, and they had raised the price of bread three or four times. {#bread}

His instant thought, Varma said, was: “Oh man, this is evil. This is just freaking evil.” Later he saw it as the price system at play. Instead of the first family buying up all the bread, two families could pool their money, so everybody got a couple of slices.
~ “Things are what they are,” he said, “and price controls always lead to shortages.”
stories.why: In a crisis, moral instinct and economic logic can point opposite ways. A high price rations a scarce good so it gets shared; a capped one lets the first comer take everything. {006-C14}

stories.start: I'll ask you a tangential question since you mentioned both Den Xiaoping
stories.end: term limits, dispersion of power, and a lot of that has peeled away
stories.caption: the greatest human of the last 30 years
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s question, and Ajay Shah’s answer
stories.head: We didn’t start the fire, Ken did
body: Amit Varma sometimes asks people who has had the greatest positive impact on humanity in the last 30 years. His own top candidate was Jeff Bezos, until a friend made the case for Deng Xiaoping, who lifted hundreds of millions of Chinese out of poverty.
Ajay Shah’s verdict on Deng borrowed from Zhou Enlai: “It’s too soon to tell.” {006-J06}
His own pick was Ken Thompson, the main inventor of Unix. “And we didn’t start the fire, Ken did.” {006-J07}

~ On Deng, Shah said that the intra-party democratic institutions and term limits he managed to create have peeled away. Varma held his ground: lifting hundreds of millions of people out of poverty, he said, was a staggering achievement.
stories.why: Each answer shows what its giver values most. Shah offered a related exercise: go back in a time machine to 1978 and ask what you would tell Deng, or Nehru. {#timemachine}

stories.start: I remember a couple of years back, there's an economist both of us know
stories.end: who does not believe believe in gravity is not a physicist I would trust
stories.caption: the economist who sneered at Hazlitt
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on an economist who sneered at Hazlitt’s readers
stories.head: One lesson is plenty
body: A couple of years ago, Amit Varma recalled, an economist both hosts know made a snarky comment: too many people arguing with him had only read Henry Hazlitt’s *Economics in One Lesson*. {006-S10}
This was an economist who, not surprisingly in Varma’s view, had defended demonetisation, or at least argued for a wait-and-watch approach.

Varma’s response: “That’s enough. Those people know more than you, right? They know the first principles.” You have to start there, he said, and “a physicist who does not believe in gravity is not a physicist I would trust.” {006-J11}
~ Hazlitt’s book uses basic principles to explain price controls, tariffs and inflation. It has sold more than a million copies and is available in some 40 to 50 languages, Varma said. {#hazlitt}

quote.text: Economics is not a subject that should be left to the economists.

quiz.q: What separates a good economist from a bad one, according to Amit Varma?
quiz.a: The bad one sees only first-order effects; the good one takes everything into account.

quiz.q: Amit Varma won the Bastiat Prize twice. Why is its trophy a candlestick?
quiz.a: It nods to Bastiat’s satire in which candlemakers petition to block out the sun.

quiz.q: A 20-rupee tariff lands on a 90-rupee Chinese teddy bear. What happens next?
quiz.a: It costs 110, so buyers pay 100 for the local bear instead.

quiz.q: Whom did Ajay Shah name as the greatest human of the last 30 years?
quiz.a: Ken Thompson, main inventor of Unix: “we didn’t start the fire, Ken did.”

quiz.q: Why did a friend of Amit Varma’s miss a flight from Delhi?
quiz.a: Delhi’s government had just capped Uber prices, and he could not get a cab.

quiz.q: Whose central price committee was Hayek’s *The Use of Knowledge in Society* written against?
quiz.a: The economist Oscar Lange’s, who wanted a committee to decide every price.
